keyFacts: Torque is force × distance: the newton-metre is the SI unit of torque.
One pound-force foot equals exactly 1.355817948 newton-metres.
One kilogram-force metre equals 9.80665 N·m (standard gravity × 1 metre).
Car engines quote torque in N·m (metric markets) or lb·ft (US market).
Bolt tightening specs are torque values — using the wrong unit can strip threads.

faqs.q: How do I convert lb·ft to N·m?
What is the difference between lb·ft and ft·lb?
faqs.a: For torque they mean the same thing — pound-force times foot. (Foot-pounds can also mean energy in other contexts, but torque wrenches read lb·ft.)
9.80665 N·m, because 1 kilogram-force = 9.80665 newtons and torque is force × 1 metre.

faqs.q: Why does my car manual list torque in N·m?
faqs.a: Metric markets use newton-metres as the SI unit. US manuals list lb·ft. They describe the same twisting force, just in different units.

faqs.q: Can I use this for bolt torque specs?
faqs.a: Yes for the unit math, but always confirm the final spec value in the manufacturer service manual before tightening critical fasteners.
